This includes maintaining strategic parts inventories, cultivating relationships with specialized suppliers, and planning replacement timelines that account for procurement lead times. 4.2 Looking Ahead The transition from legacy to modern infrastructure is not merely a technical challenge but a fundamental trans- formation in how our energy, building, and transportation systems operate and interact. As renewable generation, electric transportation, and smart building technologies become increasingly prevalent, the limitations of legacy devices become more acute. Equipment that once served reliably within isolated systems may now constrain the performance and capabilities of interconnected networks. This transformation creates both urgency and opportunity. The urgency stems from growing misalignments between aging infrastructure and emerging operational requirements—particularly in grid management, cybersecurity, and 15 This report is available at no cost from the National Laboratory of the Rockies (NLR) at www.nlr.gov/publications real-time system coordination. The opportunity lies in the potential for modernized systems to deliver unprecedented levels of efficiency, flexibility, and resilience. Success will require sustained commitment to infrastructure investment, continued innovation in integration tech- nologies, and thoughtful policies that balance modernization goals with economic and social considerations.
